analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax deduction employers get for spending to influence workers on union matters.
analysis.headline: The bill won 139 House cosponsors but the Ways and Means Committee never held a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies run campaigns to convince their employees not to unionize—including mandatory meetings, consultants, and legal fees after unfair labor practice charges—the tax code currently lets them deduct those costs as ordinary business expenses. This bill would deny that deduction, require employers to report the spending to the IRS, and impose penalties up to $100,000 for failing to report. The bill never moved past a committee referral, so it never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers deciding whether to form or join a union, because employer campaigns against organizing would become more expensive. Taxpayers also gain slightly, since they would stop subsidizing employer anti-union spending through lost revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Denies employers a tax deduction for any spending to influence employees about labor organizations, union elections, labor disputes, or collective action, ending what the bill calls a taxpayer subsidy of employer influence over workers' organizing decisions.

Requires employers to report these expenditures on their tax returns and levies a penalty of at least $10,000 (or $1,000 per full-time employee) for failure to report, with the penalty capped at $100,000.

Makes unreported spending nondeductible in practice by requiring itemized disclosure of dates, amounts, and whether the activity involved an unfair labor practice complaint, settlement, or court finding of coercion.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers that spend on anti-union campaigns would lose a deduction they currently claim, raising their after-tax cost of those campaigns. Union-avoidance consultants and law firms would face new reporting duties and likely less business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers running anti-union campaigns and their consultants

drawbacks.text: The definition of covered spending is broad: it sweeps in wages and general administrative costs connected to any meeting or training where labor organizations are discussed, which could make routine management communications with workers a disallowed business expense and raise compliance disputes.
It does not prohibit employer speech or campaigns; it only removes the tax deduction, so companies that highly value defeating organizing drives could still spend, just without the tax benefit.
Employers could argue it burdens legitimate workplace communication, and the mechanism reaches activities that are lawful under the National Labor Relations Act, not only conduct found unlawful.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea mirrors an existing, settled rule: businesses already cannot deduct spending to influence general public elections, and this extends that principle to influencing employees' union decisions [S3]. The main cost is that the covered-spending definition is broad enough to require careful regulations, and Treasury would have had 240 days to write them [S3]. The measure would not stop anti-union campaigns outright; it would make employers pay the full cost themselves rather than sharing it with taxpayers. On balance the tradeoff favors workers and taxpayers, though compliance design would matter.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and stayed there—the committee never held a hearing or a vote, and the Congress ended without the bill ever coming to the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross introduced the bill on September 14, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
It attracted 139 cosponsors—138 of 216 House Democrats and 1 of 224 House Republicans—but no further action appears in the record after the referral.
The Ways and Means Committee reported nothing, held no vote on the bill, and it expired at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that deduct anti-union campaign spending keep the tax benefit, and the union-avoidance consulting industry keeps both its business and its tax treatment. Workers hoping to change the cost calculus around organizing gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic—138 of 216 House Democrats signed on, while just 1 of 224 Republicans (Fitzpatrick) did—and the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.industry: Employers that run anti-union campaigns (large corporations and their law firms)
industries.note: The bill would strip the tax deduction for spending meant to influence employees on union matters, raising the after-tax cost of those campaigns. Because those campaigns work against workers' organizing rights, the industry interest runs against ordinary workers here.

The bill cites roughly $340 million a year in employer spending on outside consultants to sway workers' opinions, and would require these providers to report their clients' activities to the IRS, cutting demand for their services.

industries.industry: Labor unions and workers seeking to organize
industries.note: Employer anti-union spending would become more expensive and more visible, modestly improving the environment for organizing drives.
